utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, at least this first session. We'll have to see about the second. Judge Kwon couldn't be with us. All the accused are present, and the composition is as it was yesterday -- yes, as it was yesterday, except I don't see Ms. Tapuskovic today. Any preliminaries? Who wishes to go first? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I think this is an unopposed application to add one document to our 65 ter list. Mr. McCloskey has been good enough to indicate to me that he has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you, for the record, indicate the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's going to be 6D346.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Confirmed, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So the document will be included in your 65 ter list, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go into private session just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let's go into private session for a short while, please. Wait, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To facilitate what your senior legal officer is attempting to do, could we indicate that we do not intend to call the fifth witness next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. For that information, I was coming to you on that precisely, either now or later. Let's proceed now. Let's bring the first witness. By the way, because, again, of logistical problems that we have today, our intention is to sit roughly up to and not beyond 3.30 today. That being the case, I'm suggesting a break of 15 minutes or so at quarter to 2:00, if that is agreeable. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To state the obvious, it's clearly highly desirable to finish both these witnesses today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's our intention as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm only stating the obvious, though, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving testimony. Before you do so, you need to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Please proceed with reading out aloud your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Krgovic will ask you a few questions, and then we'll see who follows after him, what cross-examination. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zoranovic.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic, appearing for the Defence of General Gvero. I'm going to put to you questions. Since we are speaking the same language, as I told you in proofing, please make a pause between my question and your answer so that we do not overlap, so that the interpreters may interpret what we are going to talk about. Mr. Zoranovic, could you please state your full name and surname?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: My full name and surname is Nedeljko Zoranovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: My nickname is Nedjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 4th of August, 1957, the village of Vucinici [phoen], the municipality of Kladanj, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What qualifications do you have?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a car body mechanic -- or a car mechanic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is your profession now?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a professional truck driver in international transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When did you enter into service of the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd entered service in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: The Milici Brigade, and I was recorded as a member, as a soldier, in 1993 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: After that -- no, I apologise. If I may correct myself. I entered the military brigade in 1992. I apologise. My mistake. After that, in 1993 I came to the Main Staff. I cannot recall the date or the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which duty did you perform?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: As a driver. My duty at the Main Staff was that of a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Until when were you a driver at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of the war, I remained as a driver at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a specific task to be somebody's permanent driver or were matters arranged differently?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I had no specific duties. I was not assigned to any general or officer. I was the driver to all of them, both General Mladic, General Gvero, General Milovanovic. I drove as ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The end of July 1995, did you drive General Gvero to the UNPROFOR check-point in the area of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the date?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the date. I cannot recall the exact date, but I know that on that one occasion, I drove him to the check-point, the UNPROFOR check-point there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: General Gvero and his escort, Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the permanent driver of General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: General Gvero's permanent driver was Dragan Rajak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why he did not perform his duties those days?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but he was absent. And since I was in that unit, I was assigned to that task. I was sent to drive General Gvero on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you drive General Gvero on some other occasion to the Zepa area those days at the end of July?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was the only occasion. This was the only time that I drove him in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, when did you depart on your journey?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was the time of day?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I think around noon. I cannot be more specific. During the day, around noon, maybe in the afternoon, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you -- I apologise. First of all, where did you depart from?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: We departed from Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How long did the trip take?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: It took us some one hour to the UNPROFOR check-point, maybe even more than one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Gvero, his escort, tell you what was the purpose of your trip?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew, approximately. To reach General Mladic, we were supposed to have a brief encounter with him, and that we would be going back shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the check-point, where were you while there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at the check-point, I stayed by my car. This is my duty. Regardless of who I'm driving or wherever I am, I'm duty-bound to stand by the car to -- for security reasons, to care for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the people in the field next to the road? Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people I recognised; General Mladic, General Krstic. I saw Legenda, it seemed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Legenda," who do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: The man from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you hear what was spoken between those people? How far away were you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't hear what they spoke about. I was standing by my vehicle. And since I could park my car wherever I wanted, I parked it in the shade, and I stood by it. I could not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the buses that were passing by?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see buses passing by. They were at a distance from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be very specific, but very briefly, maybe an hour or so. We didn't stay there very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where was General Gvero's escort, where was he?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was close to him. He's his bodyguard, and this is where he's supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you set off back, did anybody tell you where you were going and which route to take?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody else but my superior officer tells me anything, and at that time it was General Gvero. He just told me, We're going back to Han Pijesak. And when we got there, he told me we would be going on a longer trip, We are going to proceed to Banja Luka, and this is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, departing and going back, I mean, between Han Pijesak and the check-point, did you make any stops along the way?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the journey from Rogatica to the UNPROFOR check-point, were there any VRS check-points?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do when you arrived back to Han Pijesak? Which route did you take, and did you stay there a while?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at Han Pijesak, we stayed there very briefly. I was told that I was going on a longer trip to Banja Luka, and after that we departed for Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stop at Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We dropped by the Drina Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a driver, I stood by my vehicle. I stayed outside. General Gvero went where he went, and there I took another vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness 6D346, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a careful look at this document. Please take note of the date in the upper left-hand corner. What the date is.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: The 26th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see your name on this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that event. Now, whether I -- or, rather, I remember that I took over a Pajero vehicle from Dragomir Vukosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you then proceed in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We took this vehicle and drove to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And why did you need this car?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's my assumption -- it's an all-terrain vehicle, and you can go anywhere in it. You can tour everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When did you reach Banja Luka; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall, but it was in the afternoon. I don't recall the exact time, but in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How far is Han Pijesak from Banja Luka? How long would it take you to drive?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from Han Pijesak to Banja Luka, it's about three or four hours to drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The way you drive it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the way I drive it, it could be less, it could be more. It all depends on the orders of the generals. Sometimes they say, Step on it, we have to be there early, and then I would do it. But sometimes it was, Let's go at a leisurely pace, and then it takes you a longer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Banja Luka on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on that occasion, I believe that we were 15 or 20 days. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen to the car that you drove in to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. As soon as we got there, the escort, General Gvero's escort, took the vehicle. I don't know whether I gave him the keys or whether he took them on his own. And he went to fill up the car, and he rolled it over. That's why I really remember this event quite clearly:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it none Defence teams wishes to cross-examine this witness. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. My name is Peter McCloskey. I represent the Prosecution in this case. Were you shown the video of Boksanica with General Gvero, and the Muslim buses, and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Defence counsel showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was maybe one or two months ago, something like that. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when was the first time Defence counsel spoke to you about anything?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence counsel first spoke to me sometime last year. I don't know whether it was in May or in April. I can't really recall. I don't recall the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you saw the video, did you see yourself in it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see myself on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see your vehicle in it?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not my vehicle either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you look for your vehicle or yourself while watching the video?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really try. I saw what I saw, but I didn't see myself or my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did anyone ask you to look for yourself or your vehicle while you were -- while they were showing it to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you left Han Pijesak around noon, when was it that General Gvero actually ate lunch?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really recall. He may have had lunch at the Corps Command with his associates, and I really don't remember. I was not there. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he could very well have had lunch at Boksanica with General Mladic in one of the buildings at the check-point, too; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him have lunch there, either, because it was just a meeting at the check-point, on a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he could have had lunch with the generals and you didn't see it because you were sitting over by your car the whole time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there were buildings at that -- at that check-point?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: There were no buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we've seen other shots of that check-point. There's actually a room -- there's a radio room. Did you ever see the radio room, go inside the radio room of the building?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go there. That's what I said, and let me say it once again. We were under orders that wherever we took the generals to, it was our duty to remain inside or beside our cars, for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, on the way -- either on the way to Boksanica or on the way back from Boksanica, did you ever stop the vehicle where there was an UNPROFOR officer along the road somewhere?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't confirm that with any certainty. I don't recall. I really don't recall making any stops or any officers stopping. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there has been evidence in this case that General Gvero, during the ten days prior to this date, was travelling different places by car.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was taking him around during that period, that ten-day period leading up to the 26th of July, which is the date we know that this Boksanica footage occurred?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to remember who drove him. I may have driven him somewhere, but you should really jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me go to 65 ter 4559. And, sir, this is a synopsis of an intercepted conversation from three days earlier, 23 July, which it's the Prosecution's position is a reliable account. It was done by the Croatian forces over the radio waves. And if you could take a moment to look at that. And I'll tell you that as we look at the substance of this, it mentions that two soldiers had been wounded that day, and we have a report in evidence here, 146, from the Drina Corps that indicates, on the 23rd of July, two soldiers were wounded in the Zepa operation. We also have indications that -- from a commander taking part in that operation, that there was a bridgehead on 23 July. And we've recently identified that there was an old rail line before the war in Zepa. And so when I read this, I want to ask you -- you asked me to refresh your recollection: "An unknown participant, who today, on 23 of July 1995, escorted General Gvero during a battle-field inspection at Zepa, said the following regarding the situation in the enclave. 'From the beginning of the Serb attack on Zepa, 17 Serb soldiers were wounded, including two from today. The progress of the Serbs is halted currently at a bridgehead and the railway tracks.'" Now, if you had been driving him on this day, this would have been a battle-field inspection, which meant that you might have been in the line of fire. So I'm sure you remember that.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I cannot confirm that I drove him on that date or, indeed, that I didn't drive him, but it's more likely that I didn't. This is unfamiliar to me. I can't tell you anything about it. The only thing that I perhaps can correct here, and I find it a bit odd, that it says here the "railway line" or the "railroad tracks." As far as I know, there are no tracks in Zepa, as far as I know. Well, but as a driver, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me go to 65 ter 4587, and I'll give you a hard map of this version. It's an old map, it's from 1959, and it's our view that there are railway -- a railway line is the dotted black-white-black-white line that you can see begins on the left side of the picture and goes down through trig point 862, then goes over near trig point 997, and you can see it twisting around. Whether it's an old rail line from a mine or something else, I don't know, but did you ever see any kind of old abandoned rail line or railroad setup in that area?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw anything, any railroad tracks, any railway lines, anything that had to do with railways there, so I can't really tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, clearly the Muslims were there until the 26th of July. Did you ever get in that area after that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not go there after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then let's go to a few days before that, the 20th of July, roughly a week, maybe -- well, six days before Boksanica. You'd been to the Jela Restaurant? It's abandoned and -- well, it was the last time I was there, anyway. Do you know where the Jela Restaurant is, sort of out in the field, not far from Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me the name of the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Jela."

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, it sounds familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think the officers of the VRS used it for functions, ate there. It was not far from HQ. I'm sure you've eaten there yourself. Right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Jela was not a restaurant for just the officers and us drivers. Anyone could go there and eat or drink and pay for the food and drinks. It was just a normal kind of restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. And did you drive anyone there on the 20th of July? I can tell you, General Mladic was there, General Gvero was there, General Milovanovic was there, General Krstic was there. That's just to name a few. It was a big party as a send-off for General Zivanovic, and there were a lot of drivers there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember that. I do remember being there on one occasion. I drove somebody there, I don't remember who, and then I went back to my command post. I simply drove somebody there and went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you have any memory of driving anyone on the 20th of July, just six days before Boksanica, which you obviously have a memory of, even though you weren't even on the tape?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't confirm that. I don't remember. It was a long time ago. Fifteen years have passed, and it's very difficult for me to say, so I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, now let's go to the 16th of July, a few days before that. And if we go to P02942, this is also in evidence in this case, and it is a UN document that indicates that -- it should be the -- 2942 is -- it is 2942. Ms. Stewart has it on her screen, so -- there we go. And we can -- and if we can -- this gives us an idea. It's a code cable dated 17 July. But if we could flip to the second page in the English, under -- it's actually the next page in the English. It should be page 3 in the English. That's it, and it's 3 in B/C/S. This is one of the records of at least one or two others that I won't take the time to show you that shows that General Gvero, on the 16th, was meeting at the Jahorina Hotel with UNHCR. Now, is there a Jahorina Hotel in Pale or Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a Jahorina Hotel at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'm sure you took senior officers there to meet with various international organisations while you were there as a driver, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. How about 16 July, some ten days before you recall taking General Gvero to Boksanica? If you thought about this, do you recall taking him to Pale, all the way over to Pale, to meet with the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say this again. We, the drivers, were very busy. We couldn't -- we didn't know anything about dates or meetings because we, and I as a driver, don't know anything about that, because nobody told us, We're going there to meet such and such a person, or to go there. They would just tell us, Drive to Pale. And once we got there, the senior officer, Gvero or whoever, would leave the car and go to those buildings, and we didn't know where he went or what he did. We stayed by the car, guarding the vehicle. And I can't really tell you whether I drove him or didn't. I cannot remember that, because we were very busy. We would sometimes -- well, I would sometimes drive General Gvero, just to give you an example, to Pale, and then come back to Han Pijesak, and then I would have to drive other officers to other places. We really worked hard, we were very busy, and we can't really know anything about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, surely you would remember, if you took General Gvero to the Srebrenica battle line, to a little forward command post out in the woods overlooking Srebrenica, when the fight was going on on July 9th, a few days earlier.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now you reminded me of the 9th of July. I can recall one occasion when I drove -- well, I don't know whether that was the date or not, I can't really claim that, but I did drive General Gvero to Belgrade. And I was there with him in Belgrade, and I can -- I seem to be able to recall that on our way back, between Vlasenica and Zvornik, I don't know whether he stopped somewhere. But it was just a very brief stop, and I can't really say where it was, who he visited, what he talked about. I was not duty-bound to know any of that. It was my duty to just drive the general where I'm told and then to bring him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this was July 9th that you took him to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the exact date, well, I can actually say that with some certainty, because I can recall when it was that I got back from Belgrade. I went straight home. I had some days off because the 12th of July is my family feast, our Patron Saints feast, and that's why I took those days off and I went home to celebrate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you tell -- you must have told the Defence attorneys about this trip to Belgrade on July 9th that you took with General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did say that. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did they suggest you might need to testify about that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they did tell me, If you are questioned, you only need to say what you know. And I shared with you everything that I know. I can't go beyond that. A long time has passed, and it's too long for me to be able to have a very clear memory of it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I ask the Defence to get proofing notes from that session where he told them about going to Belgrade on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I made an error yesterday, Your Honour. If Your Honour recalls --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we should do this without the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you understand English, Mr. Zoranovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you to remove your headphones, please. Thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As Your Honours will recall, yesterday the Court reminded the Defence that we hadn't put a number of these witnesses on our 65 ter list, and I said that two had been on the list. I made an error. Three had been on the list. The third was this gentleman. So he was on our list of last year. And for what it's worth, I don't have it in front of me, but the 65 ter summary dealt with the events of the 9th of July at Pribicevac. So it was our original intention to call him as part of the Defence case, that we then, for wont of a better word, abandoned. As the Court knows, we decided not to call any evidence at that particular juncture. And he was on the list in that regard. So that's the first thing to bear in mind. We then submitted the new list, as the Court is well aware, in relation to the new evidence, and for reasons that I'd rather not go into at the moment, largely because I maintain they're privileged, we chose not to ask him about the events of the 9th of July. My learned friend is quite entitled to cross-examine him about it, and he's doing that, but we submit we're under no duty whatsoever to produce proofing notes so far as matters that relate to things we are not asking him about. Where, I asked my learned friend, do the Rules say we have to supply that information to him? We have to supply statements, and as I made clear yesterday, we did that so far as yesterday's witness is concerned. There's no statement in existence, and we're under no duty to provide a proofing note or our own notes, which are privileged in the extreme, I submit, in terms of our dealing with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey, shall we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have about a five-line blurb from Mr. Josse on that point, and if that's what he wants to submit, that's what I'll take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, when did you first tell the Defence about your July 9th trip?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the first time, I think it was last year, when we met for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we received that note in a filing of 30 April 2008, so it would have had to have been before that. So how long before spring-time or April did you meet with them and discuss that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it might have been that date. I really don't know. I don't remember the dates, but it's possible that -- well, it may have been on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, who did you go with? Who was his personal escort then?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Gvero, when he went to Belgrade, he did not have an escort. He just went there in a car with a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how were you able to remember that you took him there on July 9th?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, there is something that I have just remembered. His father-in-law -- I took his father-in-law to Negotin. Well, I remember him as an elderly gentleman, very neat in his appearance and behaviour, and we talked about all kinds of things. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is: You would have been going back many, many years, 11, 12 years. Thinking back on what you did that -- earlier, did you review any log-book, any diary?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't keep any records, apart from when we went to Serbia, we would get some kind of a travel order to get fuel. That's the only thing that I remember. I don't remember there being anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did someone tell you -- someone remind you that you'd actually picked him up on 9 July?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you please be more specific? I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sometimes what happens, when someone contacts a witness, they may sit down with a lawyer who says, You remember where you were on 9 July, 1995, when you took General Gvero to someplace, and then ask you if you remember taking him someplace in July. They might give you a date; they might leave it open; they might show you something. How did that happen? Or you may have got a call from General Gvero from jail, or a family member, or a friend. It's normal.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, yes, I said I remembered the 9th of July because I got days off. And we returned on the 9th of July, and I was given some days off to celebrate my Patron Saints Day on the 12th of July. From that day onwards, I cannot recall the exact number of days off that I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When you came driving back, you say, from Belgrade on 9 July -- correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be so, to the best of my recollection. I used the 12th of July, my Patron Saints Day, as a reference point. We returned in good time for me to be with my family to celebrate my Patron Saints Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Around what time did you leave Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot recall the exact time, but it must have been in the afternoon, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us where you went. You're a driver, you're a professional driver. You know your routes, you know the towns, the villages. Tell us where you went. I don't need all the villages. Did you go Belgrade-Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, we went through Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from Zvornik, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: From Zvornik, we took the normal route, Zvornik to Vlasenica, through Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you got to Konjevic Polje, did you turn towards Bratunac or towards Milici and Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I cannot be specific as to what I recall. We went and stopped, but I cannot recall exactly where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Listen to my question. When you got to Konjevic Polje, did you head towards Bratunac or towards Milici? The Court's very familiar with these places, so just tell us which way you went.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not turn towards Milici, because they are on the main road. I believe that we took a turn close to Konjevic Polje. I believe -- I cannot recall specifically, but I'm sure that we didn't take the Milici road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, did you go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't go through Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So after Konjevic Polje, how long did you drive until you stopped?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, it wasn't a long journey. We drove back very fast, very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, how long, after turning on -- turning off at Konjevic Polje, did you drive until you reached your -- you next stopped the car? I'm sure you know that Bratunac is some 25, 30 kilometres from Konjevic Polje, and if you didn't make it to Bratunac, you must have stopped somewhere between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, we did not go to Bratunac. Well, somewhere there, as I tell you, it's very difficult to be specific, we turned off at someplace, but then we drove back very soon afterwards to continue our journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's what I want to know, sir. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you. In Konjevic Polje or around Konjevic Polje, we did not go to Milici. We took a turn off somewhere there, but I cannot be specific, I cannot recall. It's very difficult to confirm and be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, where did you stop; around houses, around a field? And why did you stop?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall. Please do not make me invent things I cannot really recall. As I'm telling you, we took a turn, but nobody told me where would we be going. I'm told to stop. I stand by my vehicle and do as I'm told, but I cannot recall how things unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me read you what the Defence of General Gvero told us: "The witness was a driver in the VRS Main Staff who on occasions drove General Gvero. The witness will testify that in early July 1995, he took General Gvero to Belgrade for a family visit. He then collected him a few days later on 9th and drove him to Pribicevac, where they remained for about one hour. He then drove General Gvero back to Han Pijesak." Have you ever heard of the word "Pribicevac"?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the word "Pribicevac" when I was mentioned that place by the Defence counsel. It had been unknown to me before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so where did you tell the Defence counsel you took General Gvero after you turned off at Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO ZORANOVIC
utterances.text: I told the Defence the same thing, that we took a turn off the road, but I cannot recall any place called Pribicevac. I cannot recall who he was seeing there. I cannot confirm anything of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I don't have anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I suggest we have the break now. But before we do so, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Stole? Judge Prost? Mr. Zoranovic, that brings your testimony to an end. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over, and also I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you. Documents, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just that one, 6D346.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Documents, Mr. McCloskey? You used the map and you used something else toward --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The map, and that is 4587, and the famous intercept which he invited me to refresh his recollection with, 4559.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you had another one regarding the delivery of the car. That's already in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was a Defence exhibit, and the other one was already in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, I'll repeat the objection I made yesterday, relying on the Prlic decision. Your Honour, so far as the Croatian intercept is concerned, the Court's already ruled on that at T-32547, on the 10th of March of this year. I accept that arguably the position has changed somewhat in the light of this particular witness's evidence, but we rely on that ruling. In addition to that, the submissions the Court was ruling upon on that day had been made on the 29th of January of this year; in other words, before the 20th of February, when the Prlic decision came out. And in our submission, that particular intercept undoubtedly falls foul of the Appeals Chamber's decision and should not be admitted into evidence- THE COURT: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the map will flow from that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Defence continues to make these things in issue. I get asked questions by witnesses, I use the documents before me. I think the Court has absolute discretion, in these matters, to take it or not take it and to give it whatever weight or not weight that you would like, and I will just stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. We will reserve our position as we did yesterday. Actually, we have already discussed it amongst ourselves, but in the absence of Judge Kwon, I wouldn't like to make a pronouncement. Thank you. Fifteen -- how long will the next one last on examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty, thirty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It shouldn't be long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So we'll have a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Jovanovic. You're most welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you're required by our Rules to make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be testifying the truth and the whole truth. Please read that text aloud, and that will be your solemn confirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Krgovic will go first, ask you some questions. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic. May I introduce myself. My name is Dragan Krgovic, appearing for the Defence of General Gvero, and I'm going to examine you today. Please state your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My full name and surname is Sasa Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is the place and date of your birth?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Zagreb, in Croatia, on the 18th of April, 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What qualifications do you hold?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I finished my primary school in Zagreb. After that, I graduated from the Air Force Secondary School at Rajlovac near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the JNA from the 14th of July, 1990, when I graduated from the Secondary Military School.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When did you join the VRS, and which unit did you join?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Army of the Republic of Srpska in winter 1992, on the 22nd of December, 1992. The command of my unit was headquartered at the Zalozani Airport close to Banja Luka, the 89th Helicopter Mixed Squadron.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What duty do you hold then?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Technical Department of the Helicopter Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you transferred for a time, and when, to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did the so-called duty service at the Main Staff in 1993, because a helicopter for the use of the commander and the Main Staff was there, and I was transferred there in 1993. I was permanently on duty, and I stayed there until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties, in terms of this helicopter that was there? What was your position?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, I graduated a flying or pilot course for the Gazelle-type helicopter, and I was a pilot in the crew of that helicopter. The helicopter Gazelle has usually an airman and a pilot. I was the airman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat the question. What was your duty with respect to the helicopter? It's not clear from this transcript. What was your duty, and what was the duty of your colleague?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Gazelle helicopter, which was available to the Main Staff and was used by the Main Staff, personally commanded by the -- by General Mladic, had two crew members, the pilot and flight mechanic. My role was that of the flight mechanic. I maintained the helicopter, made sure that it's ready before the flight, during the flight, navigation duties. That would briefly be my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Flight engineer?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, flight engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which rank did you have during the war?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, I held the rank of sergeant first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation now?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Currently, I work at the Batajnica Airport in Belgrade in the Army of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is your rank, and what are your duties currently?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My current rank is staff-sergeant first class, and I'm a flight engineer on a transport aircraft, AN-26.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your superior officer while you were at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The crew in the helicopter were subordinated personally to the commander of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic, and we were there for his personal needs and uses. The other flights which we performed were performed pursuant to his personal order and his personal permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What duties did you perform in July 1995; the same duties or some other duties?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, I was performing the same duties as the flight engineer of the Main Staff's helicopter which was there for the commander's personal use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you fly, in July 1995, General Mladic towards Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In late July 1995, did you drive General Mladic or fly General Mladic towards the Boksanica area, where there was an UNPROFOR check-point?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how long did it last? Was it just once, and how long was it?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, we drove him there several times in that period. Well, that's the period between, let's say, the beginning of the crisis in the Zepa area, sometime on the 19th of July, until the 29th of July. I think that we actually took him there every day, to the Zepa area. Well, several times a day, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you got there, how did you take off, where did you land, and how did you go back?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could counsel please speak into the microphone. We can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you left for the Zepa area, where did you take off, and when, and when did you return to your point of origin?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, we would take off from Crna Rijeka, where the Main Staff was, that's where the helicopter was too. I was usually in the morning. So just after dawn we would go to the Boksanica area, and we would stay there until the evening, and we would be returning at dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask Ms. Stewart for some assistance. We have problems with playing videos. If a video-clip could be played. It's already in evidence. It's about Boksanica, and it's less than a minute long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that possible, Ms. Stewart? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise yourself on this footage?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's me occupying the left-hand seat in the cockpit of the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, this flight, this helicopter flight?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember most of the flights, including this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was with you in the helicopter on that day; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was General Ratko Mladic and a cameraman from the press centre of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any security detail with him?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I assume that there was, because he would sometimes take his security detail with him. Sometimes he would leave them behind, if there were some other passengers, because you can put three passengers in the rear of the helicopter. Just a moment, I'm sorry. If the general did not take his security or bodyguards with him, then usually the pilot and myself would, upon the arrival, escort the general, as his bodyguards, until his security detail arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the check-point, the UNPROFOR check-point, where did you land; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was a meadow, a clearing about 50 metres by 150 metres large, and we landed on the left-hand side, near the macadam road. It was actually to the left of the macadam road, running across the clearing, if you look in the direction of the check-point, the UNPROFOR check-point itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know General Gvero by sight, since he was also in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him on that day when this clip was recorded?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see General Gvero on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who else was present there at the clearing, meadow, next to him?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean of the officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The officers and anyone else who might have been there.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Krstic, General Tolimir, and Vinko Pandurevic was there for a very short period of time, and a man whose nickname was Legenda. I don't know his actual name. He was from the Zvornik Brigade. And there was also the commander of the Rogatica Brigade and the commanders of the local battalions deployed in that area. The interpreter was also there, a girl from the press centre, the cameraman. Colonel Dudnjik was also there. He was commander of the UNPROFOR unit headquartered there or stationed there. That's what I was able to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were no longer visible on the footage. Where were you, in relation to the people that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was my personal position, in terms of being in photographs and being recorded in any way, well, I'm simply not in favour of that. I don't have an inclination. I don't want to be photographed or filmed. So throughout the war, I always tried to be behind the camera. I didn't want to have my face -- my photographs taken. That's simply not something that I craved. So from the time we got off the helicopter, I was always behind the cameraman, but I was also close by General Mladic, who was moving about the clearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to hear any of the conversations of the people there?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of the conversations, because I was close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was General Mladic doing at the time while these people were on the clearing together with him; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he came there, first of all, because several buses were supposed to evacuate the population from the Zepa area. He wanted to check each and every bus to ensure the safety and to talk to the people. That was his priority task. That was why he was there. Some officers had been invited by him there. They were there to be given orders personally by him for some military operations that were to be taken on another part of the front-line, and that's why they were there. Well, I can tell you which officers got there for the first time. They had never been there. They got there to get orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Officers who were supposed to go to a different part of the front-line. Which ones do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic and Legenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to hear what General Mladic told them?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard snippets of his instructions, the orders that he issued to them. I could tell you, well, just very briefly. Since there was a crisis at the part of the front-line facing Drvar in Krajina, in the Bosnian Krajina, he ordered them to move elements of their unit, the Zvornik Brigade, to put a stop to an advance by the Croatian Army and to recapture Grahovo. The front-line at the time was somewhere between Grahovo and Drvar, so he ordered them to head, together with elements of their units -- of their unit, to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what General Gvero talked about with General Mladic? Were you able to hear?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Gvero came suddenly to that area that we're talking about, and he asked to talk to General Mladic. At first, General Mladic told General Gvero to move, and I understood that to mean that he was in some kind of a waiting room, so to speak; to wait until Mladic has finished his other urgent business. And then once it was done, General Mladic would talk to him. General Gvero came there because he wanted to discuss some issues with General Mladic, because for several days he had been unable to get in touch with him, because the general was avoiding contacts with any officers that were not working on Zepa or, more specifically, the Boksanica thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you know that? Did you hear that from the conversation, or is this some knowledge that you had from some other source?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic said, on several occasions, that General Gvero was trying to get in touch with him, but he didn't -- well, he had other more urgent business to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did General Gvero and General Mladic talk finally at one point?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the buses with the people left, the general approached the General Gvero, and they talked about this issue that prompted General Gvero to come to Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to hear what they were saying?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, although at one point I, as a non-commissioned officer, as a subordinate, found it a little bit unpleasant because their discussion was rather heated, and that is not something that a subordinate officer was supposed to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was said, very briefly. To the best of your recollection, what was the course of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Gvero had been aware of the crisis at the Krajina front-line for a couple of days, and since the general is from that part of Republika Srpska, he wanted, as a general, to assist in stabilising that part of the front-line with his presence, with his presence as a general. But he couldn't leave the Main Staff without the approval of his commander. He asked the general to let him go to Mrkonjic Grad, and at one point he said something that even General Ratko Mladic accepted at one -- at a later stage. He said, I am wasting time here with 10 or 12 Muslim villages, and at the same time two towns with the greatest majority of Serbs fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And how did the conversation end?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic was angry after that conversation, but he did give his oral approval to General Gvero. He said to him, literally, Go and report to Milovanovic. Pack yourself and go and report to Milovanovic, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did General Gvero leave?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, immediately, and we stayed in that area, the Boksanica area, until the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that area, in Zepa area, after that? Did you at one point leave that area and go somewhere else in those days?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, well, we stayed there for a few days. And in the meantime, the events in Krajina became increasingly more dramatic and alarming, and the general decided to personally go to that part of Republika Srpska to be able to analyse the situation, the developments, and to do something to recapture those two towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember when you actually left for Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in the period between the 26th and the 29th, did General Mladic go to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did he stay there?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the same procedure. We would go there in the early morning, and we would remain the whole day, until the evening. In fact, one day, because of the necessity, he didn't want to go back to Crna Rijeka, to the Main Staff, but he remained in Borika. He spent the night there in a house. It was a large weekend home that belonged to Dzemal Bijedic, a former official -- high-ranking Communist official in Bosnia, and we spent a night there. We, the crew, the two of us, spent the night together with him in a room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go on the 29th, to what part of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first order issued to us by the general was to fly him by helicopter to Bijeljina, to the East Bosnia Corps Command. The flight of the helicopter through the corridor was quite risky. It was not safe at all. We reached Bijeljina, and at the time when the helicopter was about to land he decided that we should fly on to Banja Luka, because he was in a hurry, and it would take him several hours to get there by car. And so we flew over the corridor by helicopter, and we landed in the barracks where the Air Force Command was in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, the general stayed there very briefly. And after that, we flew to the command post of the 2nd Krajina Corps at Ostrelj. It's a saddle between Petrovac and Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Closer to Drvar?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, closer to Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion when you saw General Gvero, did you see him earlier, coming to the Boksanica area while you were there?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The only time that General Gvero came to the Boksanica area was on that occasion which I described. He stayed there very briefly. He waited to have a word with the general, and after this very brief conversation he left. And before or after that, he did not visit the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Another clarification. When you asked -- where asked about the fall of those towns -- I was saying "they were falling," and it says in the transcript that they had fallen, those -- the most Serb towns.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. A moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. This sentence that Mr. Gvero uttered, when did you hear it afterwards rendered by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That sentence was uttered by General Gvero, and General Mladic was angry when he heard it. But afterwards, having slept on it, he understood the meaning of that sentence, and the next time I heard that sentence was out of the words of General Mladic, when we landed at Ostrelj, the Command of the 2nd Krajina Corps. He literally said to the corps commander and those present -- he repeated that same sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're losing time, about 10 or 12 Muslim villages, and you've lost, too, most Serb of the towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we repeat what -- how I heard it: "You are wasting time on two -- 10 to 12 Muslim villages, while two of the most Serb towns are falling."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough from what he stated earlier. Let's proceed and conclude, Mr. Krgovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose no questions -- Mr. Haynes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic. I'm going to ask you just a few questions on behalf of Vinko Pandurevic. You've told us there was a girl present at Boksanica on the day that you were there. Had you seen her before, or did you see her on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I used to meet her earlier. She was part of the press centre of the Main Staff. Her name was Tanja. That's as far as I knew. She was there at the Main Staff from the beginning of the war as interpreter for English. General Mladic took her with him to Boksanica on several occasions to conduct conversations with the UN officers, and she interpreted those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I thank you for that answer. You've saved me asking you about four more questions. So we can take it, can we, that on the day of the video, General Mladic anticipated he would require translation into English?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that he had envisaged. In my post, I could not know anything about that, but maybe he had arranged for a meeting with the UN officers who'd been supposed to come to the Boksanica area. But her presence there indicated that there might be some conversations, but maybe she was there for a "just-in-case" purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you now recall whether, in fact, on that day General Mladic met General Smith?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he met General Smith on that day. I know that he had a meeting with General Smith at the Jela Motel on the main road from Han Pijesak to Sokolac and that he talked to him in the Boksanica area. I cannot recall the exact date when Smith arrived, but I recall his arrival and his entourage's arrival or his security detail's arrival, because I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Two other things. That was the only occasion you saw Vinko Pandurevic at Boksanica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SASA JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only occasion. I knew him by sight as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, and this is why I recognised him. But this was the only time that I saw him at Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. No one else from the Defence teams? None. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is -- all this information is brand new to me. I have about a maybe ten-line report on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of how much importance is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The locations and flights of General Mladic, these are very important areas, potentially. And when I study them, I'll have a chance to cut the wheat from the chaff. And we're not going to finish today, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He'll stay here and come back Monday. I mean, there's no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Mr. President. I don't know why I don't have a proofing note. I don't know why all this information, orders to Vinko Pandurevic, didn't come to us. I'm at a loss. But if I can have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go for half an hour, and then we'll continue Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you at least proceed with part of your cross-examination today or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was going on that you'd said we were stopping at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would prefer to do it all at once so I can study it. I'm completely unprepared, I've got to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then if you can check, what's our schedule Monday, morning or afternoon? I think it's in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's in the morning. We'll continue Monday morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
